prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistan's president has defended his government's recent ceasefire in the country's volatile Swat Valley in a Wall Street Journal opinion piece, saying that many in the West have mischaracterized the deal. President Zardari also said that the cease-fire would not close girls' schools in the troubled region. The permanent ceasefire, which was brokered in late February between members of the Taliban and leaders of Swat Valley, has been criticized and called a major concession by the Pakistani government in an attempt to hold off Taliban attacks. The central government has long exerted little control in the area, but it launched an intense military offensive in late July to flush out militants from areas of the North West Frontier Province . As retaliation for the military presence, the Taliban carried out a series of deadly attacks, beheadings and destruction of girls' schools. They also continued to gain ground, setting up checkpoints throughout the area. President Asif Ali Zardari addressed the international criticism in his Wall Street Journal article, published Wednesday. "We have not and will not negotiate with extremist Taliban and terrorists," Zardari wrote. "The clerics with whom we have engaged are not Taliban. Indeed, in our dialogue we'd made it clear that it is their responsibility to rein in and neutralize Taliban and other insurgents." The deal was brokered by Sufi Mohammed, a pro-Taliban cleric who in the past was arrested for leading thousands of fighters against the United States in Afghanistan. Mohammed made the deal with his son-in-law and Taliban commander Maulana Fazlullah. In the article, Zardari also said that the cease-fire would not close girls' schools in the region. "We have not and will not condone the closing of girls' schools, as we saw last year when militants closed schools in pockets of Swat Valley. Indeed, the government insists that the education of young women is mandatory. This is not an example of the government condoning or capitulating to extremism -- quite the opposite," Zardari wrote. The cease-fire deal imposes Islamic law, or sharia, in the region. As part of the agreement, the Taliban is allowing boys' schools to reopen and the government to set up temporary quarters for the more than 200,000 Swat residents who fled. Women in the area interviewed by CNN said that they would not be able to go to the schools and that, under Taliban-imposed sharia law, they cannot even be seen in public without their husbands or fathers. Swat Valley, located in North West Frontier Province, was once one of Pakistan's biggest tourist destinations. It is near the Afghanistan border and is 300 kilometers (186 miles) from the capital, Islamabad. -- CNN's Stan Grant contributed to this report.

President Asif Ali Zardari also said the ceasefire would not result in the closure of girls’ schools in the troubled region.

The permanent ceasefire, brokered in late February between Taliban members and leaders in the Swat Valley, has drawn criticism and has been described as a major concession by the Pakistani government in an effort to prevent further Taliban attacks.

The central government has long exercised limited control over the area, but in late July it launched an intense military offensive to drive militants out of parts of the North West Frontier Province. In retaliation for the military presence, the Taliban carried out a series of deadly attacks, beheadings, and the destruction of girls’ schools. The group also continued to gain ground, setting up checkpoints throughout the area.

Zardari addressed the international criticism in his *Wall Street Journal* article, published Wednesday.

“We have not and will not negotiate with extremist Taliban and terrorists,” Zardari wrote. “The clerics with whom we have engaged are not Taliban. Indeed, in our dialogue we’d made it clear that it is their responsibility to rein in and neutralize Taliban and other insurgents.”

The agreement was brokered by Sufi Mohammed, a pro-Taliban cleric who was previously arrested for leading thousands of fighters against the United States in Afghanistan. Mohammed reached the deal with his son-in-law, Taliban commander Maulana Fazlullah.

In the article, Zardari also reiterated that the ceasefire would not lead to the closure of girls’ schools in the region.

“We have not and will not condone the closing of girls’ schools, as we saw last year when militants closed schools in pockets of Swat Valley. Indeed, the government insists that the education of young women is mandatory. This is not an example of the government condoning or capitulating to extremism — quite the opposite,” Zardari wrote.

The ceasefire agreement imposes Islamic law, or sharia, in the region. As part of the accord, the Taliban is allowing boys’ schools to reopen and permitting the government to establish temporary housing for the more than 200,000 Swat residents who fled.

Women in the area interviewed by CNN said they would not be able to attend the schools and that, under Taliban-imposed sharia law, they cannot even appear in public without their husbands or fathers.

Swat Valley, located in the North West Frontier Province, was once one of Pakistan’s leading tourist destinations. It lies near the Afghanistan border and is 300 kilometers (186 miles) from the capital, Islamabad.

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — In an opinion article published in The Wall Street Journal, Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari defended his government’s recent ceasefire agreement in the unstable Swat Valley, arguing that many Western observers had misunderstood the arrangement.

Zardari also stated that the truce would not lead to the closure of girls’ schools in the troubled area.

The lasting ceasefire, arranged in late February between Taliban representatives and Swat Valley leaders, has drawn criticism from those who view it as a significant concession by Pakistan’s government aimed at reducing Taliban attacks.

Pakistan’s central government has had limited authority in the region for a long time. However, in late July it began a major military operation to drive militants out of parts of the North West Frontier Province. In response to the army’s deployment, the Taliban launched a series of lethal assaults, carried out beheadings and destroyed girls’ schools. The group also expanded its influence, establishing checkpoints across the area.

In his Wall Street Journal piece, released Wednesday, Zardari responded to the international criticism.

“We have not and will not negotiate with extremist Taliban and terrorists,” he wrote. “The clerics with whom we have engaged are not Taliban. Indeed, in our dialogue we'd made it clear that it is their responsibility to rein in and neutralize Taliban and other insurgents.”

The agreement was mediated by Sufi Mohammed, a cleric supportive of the Taliban who had previously been arrested after leading thousands of fighters against U.S. forces in Afghanistan. Mohammed negotiated the deal with Maulana Fazlullah, his son-in-law and a Taliban commander.

Zardari further emphasized in the article that the ceasefire would not result in girls’ schools being shut down.

“We have not and will not condone the closing of girls' schools, as we saw last year when militants closed schools in pockets of Swat Valley. Indeed, the government insists that the education of young women is mandatory. This is not an example of the government condoning or capitulating to extremism -- quite the opposite,” Zardari wrote.

Under the ceasefire arrangement, Islamic law, or sharia, is introduced in the region. The deal also includes provisions allowing boys’ schools to resume classes and permitting the government to create temporary shelters for more than 200,000 residents who escaped the violence in Swat.

Women from the area who spoke with CNN said they would not be permitted to attend school and that, under the Taliban’s version of sharia law, they could not appear in public unless accompanied by their husbands or fathers.

Swat Valley, situated in North West Frontier Province, was formerly one of Pakistan’s leading tourist areas. It lies close to the Afghan border and about 300 kilometers, or 186 miles, from Islamabad, the Pakistani capital.

CNN’s Stan Grant contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about President Asif Ali Zardari defending Pakistan’s Swat Valley ceasefire deal in a Wall Street Journal op-ed, including criticism over sharia law, girls’ schools, and Taliban involvement.
counterfactuals.output:
**Zardari defends Swat cease-fire deal amid criticism over Taliban gains**

*CNN-style report*

Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari defended his government’s controversial cease-fire agreement in the country’s Swat Valley, arguing in a Wall Street Journal opinion piece that the deal was a tactical effort to restore peace rather than a concession to extremists.

The agreement, reached in the northwestern region once known as a tourist destination, allowed for the implementation of Islamic law, or sharia, in parts of Malakand Division, including Swat. In exchange, militants were expected to lay down their arms after years of violence that had included bombings, executions and attacks on security forces.

Critics in Pakistan and abroad warned that the deal risked legitimizing Taliban-linked militants and surrendering authority in the region. Human rights advocates also raised alarms over the fate of women and girls, pointing to the destruction of girls’ schools and threats against female education during the Taliban’s campaign in Swat.

In his op-ed, Zardari pushed back against those concerns, saying Pakistan remained committed to fighting extremism and protecting its people. He argued that the cease-fire should be judged by whether it brought stability to a region battered by conflict, and said the government would not allow militants to impose their will by force.

The deal drew particular scrutiny because Taliban fighters had already exerted influence in Swat, enforcing harsh rules, intimidating residents and targeting symbols of the state. Many families fled the valley as violence intensified, and girls’ education became one of the most visible casualties of the insurgency.

Western officials expressed unease that the agreement could provide militants with a safe haven close to Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad. Some Pakistani liberals and civil society groups also condemned the introduction of sharia-based courts under pressure from armed groups, saying it undermined constitutional protections.

Supporters of the deal, however, said the government had few immediate options after repeated military operations failed to secure lasting peace. They argued that local demands for faster justice had been exploited by militants and that a negotiated settlement could separate reconcilable factions from hard-line Taliban elements.

Zardari’s defense came as Pakistan faced mounting pressure to show that it could confront extremism while maintaining civilian authority. The debate over Swat became a broader test of the government’s strategy: whether accommodation could reduce violence, or whether it would embolden militants seeking to expand their reach.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a news report from Islamabad on Pakistan’s government defending its ceasefire with clerics in Swat Valley, including background on Taliban attacks, Sufi Mohammed, Maulana Fazlullah, and displaced residents.
counterfactuals.output:
**ISLAMABAD —** Pakistan’s government defended its ceasefire agreement with Islamist clerics in the Swat Valley on Tuesday, insisting the deal was a necessary step toward restoring peace in a region battered by Taliban violence, military operations and the displacement of thousands of residents.

Officials said the truce, negotiated with religious leader **Sufi Mohammed**, was intended to halt fighting and bring stability to the northwestern valley, once one of Pakistan’s most popular tourist destinations. Under the arrangement, the government agreed to implement Islamic law in parts of the Malakand region, including Swat, while militants were expected to lay down arms and end attacks.

Government representatives rejected criticism that the accord amounted to a surrender to extremists, saying force alone had failed to protect civilians. They argued that the agreement could isolate hard-line militants if local clerics and residents backed peace.

Swat has been the scene of a violent campaign led by **Maulana Fazlullah**, Sufi Mohammed’s son-in-law, whose Taliban faction gained influence through fiery radio broadcasts calling for strict religious rule. His followers attacked security forces, bombed schools—particularly girls’ schools—and targeted police, government officials and opponents. Public executions and intimidation drove many residents from their homes.

Military offensives in the valley over the past year killed militants but also caused heavy disruption. Markets closed, roads became unsafe and families fled to safer areas in Pakistan’s northwest and beyond. Displaced residents have voiced mixed reactions to the ceasefire: many say they are desperate for an end to bloodshed, while others fear the militants will use the pause to regroup and impose harsher control.

Sufi Mohammed, who heads the Tehreek-e-Nifaz-e-Shariat-e-Mohammadi movement, has long campaigned for Islamic courts in the region. He previously led thousands of volunteers into Afghanistan after the 2001 U.S.-led invasion and was later imprisoned in Pakistan before being released as part of efforts to negotiate peace.

Opposition figures and rights groups warned that any deal with militants must protect constitutional rights, especially those of women and girls. International allies have also expressed concern that concessions in Swat could embolden Taliban factions elsewhere in Pakistan’s northwest, near the Afghan border.

Pakistani officials, however, said the agreement would be judged by whether militants stopped attacks and allowed normal life to resume. “The people of Swat need peace first,” one official said. “If this brings peace, it must be given a chance.”

For families who fled the valley, the question remains whether the ceasefire will bring a durable settlement—or simply mark another pause in a conflict that has repeatedly returned to their doorsteps.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.output:
**Zardari: Pakistan Has Not Negotiated With Taliban, Will Not Allow Girls’ Schools to Close**

*By CNN Staff*

Pakistan’s president, Asif Ali Zardari, said his government has not negotiated with extremist Taliban militants and insisted that girls’ schools will not be shut down under a ceasefire agreement in the country’s restive Swat Valley.

Speaking amid international concern over a peace deal in the northwestern region, Zardari said Pakistan remains committed to fighting extremism and protecting basic rights, including girls’ education.

“We have not negotiated with the Taliban,” Zardari said, stressing that any agreement in Swat must not undermine the authority of the Pakistani state or allow militants to impose their will on local communities.

The Swat Valley, once a popular tourist destination, has been the scene of intense violence as Taliban-linked militants expanded their influence, attacking security forces, government officials and schools. Girls’ schools in particular have been targeted, with militants warning families not to send daughters to class.

The ceasefire agreement, reached with local religious leaders and authorities in Pakistan’s northwest, has raised fears among critics that the government is conceding too much ground to militants. Some human rights groups and Western officials have expressed concern that the deal could allow hard-line interpretations of Islamic law to replace civil authority in the region.

Zardari rejected suggestions that the agreement would permit extremists to close schools or restrict women’s rights.

“There is no question of allowing girls’ schools to be closed,” he said. “Pakistan will not surrender to extremists.”

Pakistani officials have described the Swat arrangement as an effort to restore peace and bring stability to an area where years of fighting have displaced thousands of civilians. They say the government’s goal is to separate local grievances from militant violence while maintaining the state’s authority.

But opponents of the deal argue that previous ceasefires with militants have given extremist groups time to regroup and strengthen their control. They warn that any agreement perceived as a victory for the Taliban could embolden militants elsewhere in Pakistan.

The United States and other allies have closely watched developments in Swat, seeing the region as part of a broader struggle against militant networks operating along Pakistan’s border with Afghanistan.

Zardari said Pakistan understands the threat posed by extremism and remains committed to defeating it.

“This is our war,” he said. “We are fighting for the future of Pakistan.”

counterfactuals.output:
**Pakistan’s Swat ceasefire draws scrutiny amid sharia deal, school attacks**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** A ceasefire in Pakistan’s Swat Valley between government forces and Taliban-linked militants has brought a fragile calm to the once-popular tourist region, but the deal has drawn concern from rights groups and Western governments because it includes the imposition of Islamic law.

Under the agreement, authorities in Pakistan’s North West Frontier Province moved to introduce sharia-based courts in the Malakand division, including Swat, in exchange for militants halting attacks and laying down arms. Supporters of the deal say the measure could restore order in an area where the formal justice system had largely collapsed. Critics say it amounts to a concession to extremists who have used violence to enforce their rule.

The Taliban’s campaign in Swat has included public executions, intimidation of local officials and residents, and a sustained assault on girls’ education. Militants have destroyed or damaged scores of girls’ schools, forcing thousands of students from classrooms and prompting fears that the ceasefire could legitimize Taliban restrictions on women and girls.

President Asif Ali Zardari has defended Pakistan’s broader counterinsurgency strategy, arguing in an opinion article published in *The Wall Street Journal* that his government faces a grave extremist threat while also confronting economic and political instability. Zardari has urged international support for Pakistan, saying the country is fighting militants who endanger both Pakistan and the wider region.

CNN correspondents reporting from the region have described Swat as a valley transformed by militant control, with residents caught between Taliban edicts and military operations. Reports from the area have highlighted the shutdown of schools, fear among families, and uncertainty over whether the ceasefire will hold.

The United States and other governments have closely watched the agreement, wary that a safe haven in Swat could allow militants to regroup. Pakistani officials insist the deal is intended to isolate hard-line fighters and restore peace, but they have warned that military action could resume if militants violate the truce.

For residents, the immediate priority remains security. Markets have reopened in some areas and displaced families are weighing whether to return, but many remain cautious, saying the durability of the ceasefire depends on whether armed groups stop enforcing their own rules at gunpoint.
